description.value: This study used task-based fMRI to examine emotion-specific functional abnormalities during implicit emotional facial-expression processing in patients with behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia compared with healthy controls, correcting functional imaging data for voxel-wise grey matter volume differences.

value: patients with bvFTD would show decreased blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signal, following corrections for atrophy, in frontotemporal regions that are both directly affected by bvFTD pathology and critical for facial expression processing.

patients with bvFTD would show reduced BOLD signal compared with controls in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (inferior frontal gyrus) and anterior insula while viewing angry expressions, in the amygdala while viewing fearful expressions and in the insula while viewing disgusted expressions.
bvFTD patients may show increased BOLD activity reflecting compensatory efforts in regions unaffected by FTD pathology.
functional abnormalities would be present even after a whole-brain voxel-wise grey matter correction for atrophy/volume differences

value: Patients with bvFTD showed reduced activity in the inferior frontal gyrus while viewing angry expressions, along with reduced BOLD signal in the fusiform gyrus and cuneus and increased BOLD signal in the inferior parietal lobule and posterior cingulate gyrus compared with controls.

spans.text: As predicted, relative to healthy controls, patients with bvFTD showed reduced activity in the inferior frontal gyrus while viewing angry expressions (Fig. 2A). Consistent with predictions that secondary reductions would be observed in temporal-occipital visual areas in patients with bvFTD, we observed reduced BOLD signal in the fusiform gyrus (Fig. 2B) and cuneus in patients compared with controls. In contrast, we observed increased BOLD signal in patients with bvFTD compared with controls in the inferior parietal lobule and posterior cingulate gyrus (Fig. 2C).

spans.text: Consistent with the role of the insula in the processing of disgusted stimuli and the involvement of this region early in the course of bvFTD, patients with bvFTD demonstrated decreased BOLD signal in the insula in response to disgusted facial expressions (Fig. 2D). In addition, patients showed reduced activation in the lingual gyrus (extending into the fusiform cortex) and middle occipital gyrus compared with controls.
